cim: Could Artificial Intelligence Decide the Outcome of the 2028 Presidential Election?
cim_eredeti: Could Artificial Intelligence Decide the Outcome of the 2028 Presidential Election?
szoveg_eredeti:
By the time Americans head to the polls in 2028, artificial intelligence could become one of the most powerful political influences in modern history.

As platforms such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Grok and Claude grow in popularity, voters may increasingly abandon traditional internet searches in favor of asking AI direct questions about political candidates, their policies and their backgrounds.

But what happens when the companies controlling those platforms have political interests of their own?

During the 2020 presidential election, Facebook and Twitter faced widespread accusations of political bias, shadow-banning conservative voices, restricting right-leaning content and promoting narratives favorable to Democrats.

One of the most notable examples was the suppression of the New York Post's reporting on Hunter Biden's laptop just weeks before the election. Twitter blocked users from sharing the story, while Facebook deliberately reduced its distribution. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg later acknowledged that Facebook should not have suppressed the report.

While the impact on the election's outcome remains disputed, the incident demonstrated the extraordinary power technology companies wield over political information.

By 2028, AI could provide an even more powerful and less detectable means of influencing public opinion.

Unlike traditional Google searches, which provide links to multiple sources, AI platforms can deliver a single, seemingly authoritative answer. While Americans may recognize the political leanings of certain news organizations, many assume artificial intelligence provides objective, unbiased information.

An AI platform would not necessarily have to fabricate information to influence an election.

When asked about two presidential candidates, AI could emphasize one candidate's accomplishments while focusing on the other's controversies, legal troubles or policy failures.

Every statement could be factually accurate, yet the overall presentation could favor one candidate over another.

Political bias could originate from training data, internal programming instructions, corporate policies or the sources selected when generating responses.

A December 2025 study published in the scientific journal Nature examined AI's ability to influence voters during elections in the United States, Canada and Poland.

Researchers found that conversations with AI produced shifts in candidate preferences that exceeded the effects typically observed in traditional political video advertisements.

For decades, Americans have debated the political influence of newspapers, television networks and social media platforms.

AI introduces another dimension: personalized, private conversations capable of influencing millions of people simultaneously.

Unlike political advertisements or publicly accessible news articles, AI-generated responses may never be seen by anyone other than the person asking the question, making political bias more difficult to detect and document.

Furthermore, as AI becomes more familiar with individual users, their interests and preferences, it could become increasingly effective at tailoring persuasive information to each individual.

In closely contested elections, even a relatively small shift in voter preferences could determine who occupies the White House.

As 2028 approaches, questions surrounding AI transparency, political neutrality and corporate accountability could become increasingly important - not just in America, but in democracies worldwide.

The greatest concern may not be whether artificial intelligence can cast a ballot, but whether the companies controlling it could ultimately influence enough voters to decide who wins.
